entities.name: Comgall mac Domangairt
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Comgall mac Domangairt, who reigned as King of Dál Riata from approximately 500 CE until his death in 540 CE, stands as a pivotal figure in the early consolidation of Gaelic power in what would become western Scotland. Succeeding his father, Domangart mac Fergusa, Comgall's rule was instrumental in solidifying the nascent kingdom of Dál Riata, a polity straddling parts of modern-day Argyll in Scotland and Antrim in Ireland. His reign occurred during the tumultuous post-Roman period, an era defined by political fragmentation in Britain and the expansion of Gaelic influence from Ireland, establishing a crucial precedent for future Scottish identity.

During his forty-year reign, Comgall is believed to have strengthened the kingdom's territorial holdings in Argyll and perhaps extended its influence, though specific military campaigns or diplomatic achievements are not extensively detailed in contemporary annals. He is primarily remembered as the eponymous ancestor of the Cenél Comgaill, one of the three principal kindreds (Cenél nGabráin, Cenél Loairn, and Cenél Comgaill) that comprised the royal aristocracy of Dál Riata. This lineage played a significant role in the internal politics of Dál Riata, often vying for supremacy with the Cenél nGabráin, founded by his brother Gabrán mac Domangairt. The establishment and recognition of these distinct royal lines were fundamental to the kingdom's structure.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Comgall mac Domangairt's reign was crucial in consolidating the early Dál Riata kingdom, establishing a key dynastic lineage (Cenél Comgaill) that would shape the political landscape of western Scotland for centuries and contribute to the eventual formation of Alba.
